Article Title: Why the Vikings signing Jamal Adams on the eve of training camp could solve a problem no one is talking about
Article Text:
Jamal Adams joins Vikings (Getty Images)

What does Jamal Adams bring to the Minnesota Vikings defence in 2026?

Is Jamal Adams still good enough to contribute meaningfully at age 30?

Jamal Adams is heading into his 10th NFL season -- and for the first time in years, it actually feels like a clean start. The Minnesota Vikings confirmed the signing of the veteran defensive back on July 27, with Adams himself making it official on X: "Year 10. #skol." The move brings a former first-team All-Pro to a defence that lost Harrison Smith and is still figuring out its safety depth. Adams, 30, arrives having reinvented himself as a linebacker with the Las Vegas Raiders in 2025, playing 448 snaps and showing enough to earn one more shot.The easy framing is that Adams is depth. That's not wrong, but it undersells why Brian Flores specifically makes this signing interesting. Adams has never fit cleanly into a traditional safety or linebacker box -- he's too physical for deep coverage, too undersized to hold up as a full-time box linebacker. Flores, though, has spent his coaching career exploiting exactly that kind of tweener profile.With Harrison Smith's retirement leaving a gap at the backend, Josh Metellus is expected to take on a more traditional safety role alongside Theo Jackson.That pushes Adams into a different function -- a third safety option, a dime package piece, a pressure specialist who can be deployed situationally. It's the same utility role Pete Carroll designed for him in Las Vegas, and Adams took to it faster than anyone expected.During his Raiders stint, Adams registered 45 tackles, five for loss, a sack, two quarterback hits and a forced fumble in 17 games. The sack and QB hits matter most here — Adams near the line of scrimmage as a blitzing piece was the one skill that made him special during his All-Pro years with the Jets, and it still showed up in Year 9.The position switch itself deserves more credit than it gets. Adams played linebacker for the first time in his professional life last season. Carroll was blunt about it. "[Carroll] straight up told me, 'You're going to be in the linebacker room, so get over it,'" Adams told the Raiders' website in August 2025. "So I was just like, 'Alright s--t, let's do it.'"He did it. And now the Vikings are betting that same adaptability carries into a new system.It's a fair question, and the honest answer is: probably, but in a limited capacity. The version of Jamal Adams who dominated as a blitzing safety for the Jets between 2017 and 2019 -- three Pro Bowls in four seasons, first-team All-Pro in 2019 -- is not walking through the door in Minnesota. That player was traded to Seattle for a package that included two first-round picks, a price that never paid off for the Seahawks.Injuries derailed nearly everything that followed. A torn labrum, a torn quad tendon, a hip injury -- Adams played just 34 games in four seasons with Seattle. He was released after the 2023 campaign, bounced through Tennessee and Detroit in 2024 without making much impact, and looked like a cautionary tale about big contracts and bad luck.But the Raiders gave him a real opportunity, and he stayed healthy for a full season for the first time in years. That's the clearest signal the Vikings are betting on. If Adams can stay on the field, Flores has the schematic creativity to find him snaps. Minnesota also drafted Jakobe Thomas in the third round, but third-round safeties are not guaranteed contributors in Year 1. Adams gives the team a bridge option who knows how to play under pressure.The real subplot here is Harrison Smith. The longtime Vikings safety hasn't officially announced retirement, and his decision -- whenever it comes -- will shape how much Minnesota actually relies on Adams. If Smith comes back, Adams is clear-cut depth. If Smith walks away for good, this signing suddenly looks like a quiet necessity dressed up as a low-risk flier.For a player entering his sixth team, the Vikings represent something straightforward -- a chance to be useful in a defence that needs exactly what he offers. Not a star turn. Not a redemption arc. Just a professional doing his job in a system built for him.

Adams, 30, arrives having reinvented himself as a linebacker with the las vegas raiders in 2025. He registered 45 tackles, five for loss, a sack, two quarterback hits and a forced fumble.

What's next for Hernández?

Elieser Hernández's stay in Atlanta ended the way a lot of veteran bullpen arms' stints do this time of year, fast and without ceremony. He threw three scoreless innings of relief in the Braves' 7-6 extra-innings win over Baltimore on Saturday, helping stretch that game out. A day later, Atlanta designated him for assignment, even as the club opened a series with the Mets at Citi Field.Hernández cleared waivers and was outrighted to Triple-A Gwinnett. He'd been through that process before, which meant he had the option to elect free agency rather than accept the assignment, and he took it. MLB.com's transactions log confirmed the move in blunt terms: "RHP Elieser Hernández elected free agency." His three innings against the Orioles are the only MLB innings he's logged in 2026.The DFA came despite a clean outing, which says more about Atlanta's roster math than about Hernández's stuff that day. He hadn't pitched in the majors since 2024, when he split time between Milwaukee and Los Angeles and posted a rough 15.2-inning stretch, 11 earned runs allowed and five home runs surrendered.Elieser Hernández contract details with the BravesPer Spotrac, Hernández signed a one-year, $850,000 deal with Atlanta, all of it guaranteed, with an average annual value matching the base salary.There was no signing bonus attached. His 2026 payroll figure for luxury tax purposes came in at $27,270, reflecting his buried roster status for most of the season.Career-wise, Hernández holds an 11-22 record with a 5.05 ERA across 100 games and 49 starts, spanning 306.1 innings with 287 strikeouts and a 1.32 WHIP. In his lone 2026 appearance, he went 1-0 with a 0.00 ERA over three innings, striking out two batters. The Venezuela-born right-hander, nicknamed "Lilo," debuted in the majors on May 10, 2018, after Miami took him in the first round of the 2013 draft.Hernández is now a free agent, cleared to sign with any of the league's 30 clubs. Whether he lands back in Atlanta's system or elsewhere, his next outing will be his first true audition since a shaky 2024. For a pitcher with a 5.05 career ERA looking to hang on, three scoreless innings is a start, not a guarantee.

Article Title: Who are Spencer Jones’ parents? Meet the family that helped shape the Denver Nuggets forward’s remarkable NBA journey
Article Text:
Spencer Jones’ parents (Image Via Getty)

Spencer Jones ’ father Dwayne Eric Jones helped build a strong foundation

Spencer Jones turned an undrafted setback into a life changing NBA opportunity

Spencer Jones’ NBA story is very different from that of most players. He was not a first-round draft pick or a highly talked-about prospect. Instead, he went undrafted in 2024, worked his way through a two-way contract, and earned a regular NBA deal before landing a fully guaranteed two-year, $12 million offer sheet that the Denver Nuggets matched in July 2026. Behind that steady rise has been a family that valued discipline, education and hard work from the very beginning.Spencer Jones is the son of Dwayne Eric Jones, a Harvard-educated physician who has worked in cardiology. Publicly available profiles also note that Dwayne competed in track during his younger years, giving him both an academic and athletic background.While Spencer’s mother has largely stayed away from the public eye, available reporting says she briefly played basketball before choosing to keep her personal life private. Her name has not been publicly confirmed by reliable sources.Although his parents rarely speak publicly, reports suggest they created a home where discipline, consistency and education were just as important as sports. His father’s medical career and athletic experience are believed to have played a major role in teaching Spencer the value of preparation, patience and staying committed even when success takes time.Because his mother has remained private, very little verified information is available about her. For that reason, it is best to avoid claims beyond what has been publicly reported.Jones spent five seasons at Stanford, where he became one of the program’s most dependable players. He appeared in a school-record 146 games and finished as Stanford’s all-time leader with 315 three-pointers.Despite those achievements, Jones was not selected in the 2024 NBA Draft. Instead of giving up, he joined the Denver Nuggets on a two-way contract after playing Summer League basketball.The first year was not easy. He moved between the NBA and the G League while waiting for opportunities. His patience paid off in February 2026 when Denver rewarded him with a standard NBA contract.During the 2025-26 season, Jones appeared in 64 games and started 37. He averaged 5.5 points and 3.3 rebounds while shooting 39.6 percent from three-point range. His reliable shooting and defense made him an important part of Denver’s rotation.That progress caught the attention of other teams. In July 2026, the Oklahoma City Thunder signed Jones to a fully guaranteed two-year, $12 million offer sheet. The Nuggets quickly matched the offer, making it clear they saw him as an important part of their future.Jones’ story is not built around overnight success. It is about trusting the process, staying ready and making the most of every chance. The values he learned at home helped him keep moving forward, even after the disappointment of going undrafted.

Article Title: What the latest Baker Mayfield report really says about Tampa Bay's confidence in its $47 million franchise quarterback
Article Text:
Baker Mayfield (Getty Images)

Could the Buccaneers use the franchise tag instead of giving Baker Mayfield a new contract?

Baker Mayfield's contract situation in Tampa Bay is getting messier and more fascinating by the week. The Buccaneers quarterback is in the final year of a reworked deal worth $27 million in 2026, with no long-term extension anywhere close to the horizon. And now, according to ESPN's Jeremy Fowler, the franchise tag is emerging as a very real possibility for 2027 -- one that could cost Tampa Bay at least $47 million.A franchise tag has rarely been part of the public discussion around Mayfield's future, but Fowler believes it remains a realistic possibility."While Mayfield would prefer a long-term deal, he’s not afraid of the franchise tag, which would cost Tampa Bay at least $47M in 2027," ESPN's Jeremy Fowler wrote on his official X account on Sunday.From Mayfield's perspective, the financial risk appears limited. He has already earned significant money during his NFL career and is due another $40 million this season. That gives him room to be patient rather than force negotiations."Baker has made $131.8 million already in his career & he’ll make $40 million this season," Damage Inc. wrote on X on Sunday. "Getting tagged at $47 million at age 32 won’t faze him at all.I’m sure he would like another nine-digit contract, but he’s going to make over $200 million in his career regardless."While the financial side remains stable, Mayfield enters the season with something else to prove. Last year started in impressive fashion as both he and the Buccaneers looked like one of the NFL's biggest success stories through the first six weeks. That momentum faded quickly. Tampa Bay finished 8-9, missed the playoffs for the first time since 2019 and Mayfield's standing across the league took a hit.ESPN's annual survey of NFL executives, coaches and scouts reflected that shift. After previously being viewed among the league's top quarterbacks, Mayfield dropped out of the Top 10 and landed in the honourable mention category. He also missed out on the Pro Bowl after earning selections in each of his first two seasons with Tampa Bay.Even so, respect for his game has not disappeared. Mayfield was the only quarterback from the NFC South to receive votes in the rankings."Mayfield is a winner," one anonymous NFL coordinator told ESPN's Jeremy Fowler. "He can make every throw. Fearless. Teammates seem to love to play for him."Mayfield himself has made it clear that contract talks are not his immediate focus, even if discussions have not progressed as hoped."(Contract extension talks) not anywhere close to what we were thinking," Mayfield told Tampa Bay Times NFL reporter Rick Stroud. "Would love to be here long term, but as of right now that’s not exactly the case. But I’m under contract for 2026. The guys in that locker room, the staff know that I’m still gonna be me. I’m still going to do everything I can to help this team win a Super Bowl. To me, that’s the priority. Everything else will take care of itself. "For now, the Buccaneers do not appear under pressure to make an immediate decision. A strong 2026 season could strengthen Mayfield's case for another long-term deal. If not, the franchise tag offers Tampa Bay another option while keeping its starting quarterback in place.
Article Summary: Baker mayfield is in the final year of a reworked deal worth $27 million in 2026. The franchise tag is emerging as a very real possibility for 2027. Tampa bay finished 8-9, missed the playoffs for the first time since 2019.

Article Title: Inspiring story of the day: “Without the people that I have around me, all these years, without my family, without my team, it would be impossible. They give me peace of mind” - How Rafael Nadal’s fam
Article Text:
Inspiring story of the day: “Without the people that I have around me, all these years, without my family, without my team, it would be impossible. They give me peace of mind” - How Rafael Nadal’s family stood by him through every injury on his road to tennis immortality (Image via Getty)

How did Rafael Nadal overcome a career-threatening foot condition?

Why did Rafael Nadal always choose family and home over fame?

What did Rafael Nadal say about his wife and family during his injury battles?

What life lesson did Rafael Nadal learn from pain and defeat?

For years, Rafael Nadal inspired fans with his fight on the tennis court. What many people did not see was the battle he fought away from the spotlight. Long before becoming a 22-time Grand Slam champion, Nadal was told that a rare foot condition could end his career. He dealt with constant pain, serious injuries and doubts about whether he could keep playing. Yet he kept coming back. While his determination made headlines, Nadal has always said his biggest strength was the people who stood beside him. Their support helped him survive the hardest moments and build one of the greatest careers in tennis history.In 2005, Nadal won his first French Open title at just 19 years old. Soon after that breakthrough, he was diagnosed with Mueller-Weiss syndrome, a rare condition that affects the bones in the foot.Doctors warned that continuing his career at the highest level might not be possible.Instead of giving up, Nadal returned home to Manacor in Mallorca. There, he was surrounded by his father Sebastián, mother Ana María, sister Maribel and his longtime partner Mery Perelló. Their support gave him the strength to keep moving forward when his future looked uncertain.Looking back on those difficult years, Nadal once said:“Without the people that I have around me, all these years, without my family, without my team, it would be impossible.They give me peace of mind.”Despite becoming one of the biggest names in world sport, Nadal never left the place where he grew up. He stayed close to his family in Manacor and continued living the simple life that had shaped him from childhood.His uncle and longtime coach Toni Nadal taught him to stay humble, respect opponents and never believe he was bigger than the game. Those lessons stayed with him throughout his career.Nadal has often explained that returning home helped him switch off from the pressure of professional tennis. In Manacor, he was simply Rafa, spending time with friends and family. That normal life became an important part of maintaining his mental balance through the highs and lows of the sport.Nadal’s wife, Mery “Xisca” Perelló, was by his side long before he became a global star. She witnessed every comeback, every rehabilitation session and every painful setback that fans rarely saw.As injuries continued in the final years of his career, those shared sacrifices became even more meaningful. With his wife, young son and team watching from the stands, Nadal reflected on everything they had gone through together.He said:“Having my family here, my wife, my son, my team… it’s emotional because they know how hard the process has been. They have been through the good moments, but especially the tough moments during all these years of injuries.”Nadal never believed success came without suffering. Throughout his career, he played through injuries, long matches and physical pain that would have stopped many athletes. Instead of running from those challenges, he accepted them as part of the journey.That mindset became one of the biggest reasons behind his remarkable career.As Nadal explained:“If you don’t lose, you cannot enjoy the victories. You have to accept both things. I learned during my career to enjoy suffering.”His story goes far beyond Grand Slam trophies or records. It shows that true strength is not only about winning titles but also about staying grounded when life becomes difficult. Through every injury and every comeback, Nadal never lost sight of the people who mattered most. Their love gave him the peace, confidence and support to keep chasing his dreams, making his journey one of the most inspiring stories in modern sport.
Article Summary: Rafael nadal was diagnosed with a career-threatening foot condition in 2005. The spaniard returned home to manacor in mallorca to be with his family. Nadal has always said his biggest strength was the people who stood beside him. His uncle and longtime coach toni nadal taught him to stay humble.

Article Title: “Three-against-one situation”: El Rubius opens up on being “targeted” in MrBeast’s viral $1M challenge

El Rubius reflects on a tough and “unfair” exit

Abraham, if you’re watching this, we were all rooting for you, and standing right there with you."His message carried mixed emotions. There was disappointment, yes, but also pride in how he handled things. Giving away his $50,000 winnings to his community stood out as a gesture that meant more than the result itself.He continued with another honest note, saying, "And in the end, karma finally caught up with that little punk. Article Title: Quote of the day by Taylor Swift's husband Travis Kelce: "If you don't care about the guy next to you, one, you're a terrible…" - why caring about your teammates matters more than individual talent
Article Text:
Travis Kelce

Quote of the day by Travis Kelce

"If you don't care about the guy next to you, one, you're a terrible teammate. Two, you're never gonna win"

What is the meaning behind the quote by Travis Kelce

A real example of Kelce living this out

Why teamwork tends to matter more than raw talent alone

Why genuinely caring about people builds real trust

Why every single role in a team actually matters

Why caring about teammates as people improves performance

Why shared goals bring people together

Other famous quotes by Travis Kelce

"I'm a firm believer that individual accolades are a bit overrated in this game."

"My entire career, you can't say Travis Kelce without Alex Smith. He's been my quarterback, he's been the guy. I owe a lot of my success to him."

"Nobody puts more expectation on me than myself. That's just the heart of the competitor."

"As soon as you get complacent with where you are in a game, that's where you come and then it bites you in the rear. So you just want to make sure that you're keeping that energy high."

Why this quote is relevant today

People love celebrating the star player, the standout entrepreneur, the individual talent who seems to carry a whole team on their back. Travis Kelce , the NFL tight end, pushed back on that picture directly. "If you don't care about the guy next to you, one, you're a terrible teammate," he said. "Two, you're never gonna win." Individual ability clearly matters. What Kelce is pointing at is something that matters just as much and gets talked about far less, whether you actually care about the people working alongside you. It is a simple line, but it says something about winning that gets missed constantly by people focused purely on their own individual numbers."The guy next to you" is not really about friendship here. It stands for respect, trust and a genuine sense of responsibility toward the people you work with. In any team, one person's performance always affects everyone else around them, whether they think about it that way or not.Kelce makes two separate points. First, someone who does not genuinely care about their teammates is failing at one of the most basic parts of actually being on a team. Second, and just as important, that attitude tends to stop the whole group from winning anything meaningful together. Personal excellence on its own was never going to be enough, no matter how talented any single person happens to be.This is not just something Kelce says. In December 2023, his teammate Kadarius Toney committed an offside penalty that wiped out a game-winning touchdown against the Buffalo Bills. Several media figures, including Stephen A. Smith, publicly urged Kelce and quarterback Patrick Mahomes to call Toney out over the mistake. Kelce did the opposite. He defended his teammate directly and pushed back at the media instead of piling on. That is really the quote in action, not just as a line he says, but as something he actually chose to do when the pressure was on to do the opposite.Talent can shift the outcome of a single game, project or assignment, but it rarely guarantees success by itself. A group full of talented people who do not cooperate well often underperforms compared to what they should be capable of. Teams built around genuine communication and trust, on the other hand, regularly produce results that look far better than the sum of their individual parts, because real teamwork lets everyone's strengths actually complement each other instead of competing for attention.Trust builds up once people can see that their teammates actually care whether they succeed or not. A colleague who shares useful knowledge freely, a teammate who offers encouragement after a mistake instead of criticism, a leader who actually notices individual effort, all of these build confidence inside a group. Once that trust exists, people communicate more openly and become far more willing to actually help each other through a hard patch. Kelce's line is really arguing that this kind of care is not just a nice extra. It is a genuine, practical advantage, one that shows up directly in how a team actually performs when things get difficult.Winning teams are almost never the product of one standout individual working alone. In football, championships depend on players, coaches, trainers and support staff all pulling together. The same pattern shows up everywhere else too, in hospitals, in schools, in businesses. Every role genuinely contributes to the final result, and respecting each one, rather than only celebrating the most visible positions, is what actually strengthens the whole group.Treating teammates as actual people rather than simply co-workers tends to build stronger relationships across the board. That kind of empathy encourages patience after a mistake, improves communication under real pressure, and builds loyalty that holds up during difficult stretches. Performance and genuine care were never really separate things. Caring properly about the people around you tends to make everyone perform better, not worse.Strong teams focus on winning together rather than chasing individual recognition. Once people genuinely prioritise the team's goal over their own personal stats or credit, cooperation increases almost automatically, and competition inside the group tends to become healthier rather than more divisive. Success stops being something individuals fight over and starts being something the whole group actually shares.Modern workplaces increasingly depend on collaboration across different skills and backgrounds, which means technical ability on its own is rarely enough anymore. Communication, trust and genuine mutual respect have become just as important as raw skill. Kelce's quote is a reminder that relationships between teammates were never really separate from performance. They are usually the actual reason high-performing teams exist in the first place, on a football field, in an office, or anywhere else people have to rely on each other to get something done.
Article Summary: "if you don't care about the guy next to you, one, you're a terrible teammate," says nfl tight end travis kelce. Kelce's quote says something about winning that gets missed constantly by people focused purely on their own individual numbers. In any team, one person's performance always affects everyone else around them.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Oracle founder Larry Ellison: "Great achievers are driven, not so much by the pursuit of success, but by…" - a powerful lesson on ambition, failure and the mindset behind extraordi
Article Text:
Representative Image

Quote of the day by Oracle founder Larry Ellison

"Great achievers are driven, not so much by the pursuit of success, but by the fear of failure"

Understand the meaning behind Larry Ellison’s quote

Why fear of failure can actually be useful

Why success on its own is never really enough

Why continuous improvement matters more than any single achievement

Why setbacks often build real resilience

Why discipline tends to outlast raw talent

Why this is not the same as harmful anxiety

Other famous quotes by Larry Ellison

"When you innovate, you've got to be prepared for people telling you that you are nuts."

"Life's a journey. It's a journey about discovering limits."

"The most important aspect of my personality as far as determining my success goes has been my questioning conventional wisdom, doubting experts and questioning authority."

"I have had all the disadvantages required for success."

What it means in today's world

Most people assume successful individuals are pulled forward purely by ambition, chasing wealth, recognition and big wins. Larry Ellison, the co-founder of Oracle, offered a different explanation for what actually drives people to the top. "Great achievers are driven, not so much by the pursuit of success, but by the fear of failure," he said. It is not really an argument in favour of fear. It is an observation about where a lot of real discipline actually comes from, and it fits closely with how Ellison himself has described building one of the largest technology companies in the world from a much smaller and far less certain starting point.Most people picture successful individuals as motivated purely by optimism, chasing the next win with total confidence. Ellison is describing something a little different from that picture entirely. Plenty of top performers push themselves relentlessly because they understand exactly what failure would actually cost them, and rather than freezing up over that possibility, they use it to stay sharp and keep improving.The key distinction sitting inside the quote is between fear that stops someone acting at all and fear that pushes someone to prepare properly.The first shuts things down. The second is what actually keeps people sharp long after they could reasonably have relaxed.Fear usually gets treated as something purely negative, and plenty of it is. Not all fear works that way though. A healthy awareness that things could go wrong tends to make people prepare more thoroughly, practise more consistently, and think harder before big decisions. Athletes train hard precisely because they know competition will be demanding. Students revise because exams genuinely require it. In every one of these cases, the possibility of failing is exactly what pushes people to put in more effort, not less.Success has a way of creating comfort, and comfort has a way of turning into complacency. Plenty of people and organisations start declining right after they succeed, simply because they stop pushing once things feel secure. Markets shift. Technology moves on. Customer expectations change constantly. People who stop learning at that point tend to fall behind fairly quickly. Ellison's quote is really arguing that staying aware of the possibility of failure is exactly what keeps great achievers improving, even well after they have already succeeded.Real achievement is rarely the product of one single effort. It usually gets built slowly, through constant refinement, learning new skills, correcting mistakes, adapting when circumstances shift, and continuing to look for better solutions even when the current one already works fine. People who keep this habit up stay ready for whatever comes next, because they never fully stopped asking how they could be a little better than they were yesterday.Failure is rarely pleasant in the moment, yet many successful people describe it afterward as one of the most useful teachers they ever had. A failed product reveals a genuine weakness worth fixing. A rejected idea often leads directly to a better one. Resilience really develops through treating a setback as useful information rather than as a final verdict on someone's ability, which is exactly the alertness Ellison's quote is describing, an ongoing willingness to notice what went wrong instead of simply moving past it without learning anything at all.Natural ability gives someone a head start. Discipline is what actually determines whether that ability gets developed properly over time. Someone genuinely motivated to avoid failure tends to build habits around regular practice, careful preparation and continuous learning, and those habits usually end up mattering more in the long run than raw talent ever did on its own, since talent alone rarely survives the first serious setback without something sturdier underneath it.It is worth being clear about the difference here. Constant anxiety that damages confidence or actively prevents someone from trying anything is not what this quote is describing. Healthy motivation sounds like "I want to prepare properly because this genuinely matters." Unhealthy anxiety sounds like "I should not even try in case I fail." The first pushes someone into action. The second keeps them frozen in place.The pace of change today makes continuous improvement close to essential rather than simply admirable. Skills that mattered five years ago can become outdated surprisingly quickly. Ellison's quote is a reminder that lasting achievement usually depends less on celebrating a past success and more on staying genuinely committed to the next round of improvement. The awareness that failure remains a real possibility is exactly what keeps that commitment alive long after the applause for the last win has faded, which is really the whole difference between a career that keeps growing and one that quietly stalls out.
Article Summary: "great achievers are driven, not so much by the pursuit of success, but by the fear of failure" larry ellison, co-founder of oracle. Ellison argues that staying aware of the possibility of failure is what keeps great achievers improving. The pace of change today makes continuous improvement close to essential rather than simply admirable.

Article Title: 'I was beaten from 11 pm to 3 am': How Sharmila Dhankar overcame marriage abuse to script CWG history
Article Text:
Sharmila Dhankar (ANI Photo)

New Delhi:

For Sharmila Dhankar, every throw carries the weight of a life rebuilt. From growing up in poverty in Haryana’s Mahendragarh district and surviving domestic abuse in her first marriage to selling the family home to sustain her sporting dream, the 40-year-old para shot putter has turned adversity into ambition as she prepares for her second Commonwealth Games (CWG).On Monday night, Sharmila scripted history by becoming India's first-ever COmmonwealth Games para-athletics gold medallist. She delivered a landmark performance by winning the women's shot put F57 title with a season-best effort of 9.81m, ending the nation's 20-year wait for a para-athletics medal at the Games. The last para-athletics medal in CWG was won by Ranjith Kumar Jayaseelan in the men's seated discus throw event in the 2006 edition.The F57 classification is for athletes with lower limb impairments, limb deficiencies or reduced muscle power.The seated thrower, who also competes in discus, headed into the Games on the back of an impressive showing at the Fazza International Para Athletics Championship in Dubai, where she won gold in shot put and bronze in discus.Her sporting journey began only at the age of 34. Sharmila contracted polio at the age of two, affecting her right leg and grew up in a family struggling to make ends meet.“My mother was blind, my father was a farmer and we had very little to survive. Life was never easy,” she told TOI.Married at 19, she endured years of domestic violence before returning to her parents’ home with her two daughters — Anju, now 15, and Lakshmi, 13. “One night, I was beaten from 11 pm to 3 am by my first husband and thrown out of the house. I never went back,” she recalled.Her life changed after her second marriage. Husband Ajit Singh introduced her to para sports and encouraged her to train under coaches Tek Chand and Devendra. In 2021, she made her debut at the Para National Championships and won gold with a national record.The following year, she finished fourth at the Birmingham CWG, narrowly missing a medal. She placed fourth again at the Asian Para Games in Hangzhou in 2023. Despite those strong performances, financial hardship persisted. To fund her career, the family sold their house in Rewari in 2023 and moved into rented accommodation. “Sport has given me a second birth. After winning medals in para CWG and Asian Games this year, I want to buy a house again,” she said.Sharmila had finished fifth at the World Para Athletics Championships in New Delhi last year. Beyond medals, her biggest dream is to ensure that her daughters have the opportunities she never did.
